claim: The growth in scientific publishing makes it increasingly difficult for researchers to keep up-to-date with the newest trends in their fields.
source: The growth in scientific publishing (Larsen and von Ins, 2010) makes it increasingly difficult for researchers to keep up-to-date with the newest trends in their fields (Medoff, 2006; Collins, 1998).
evidence: Supported by citations to Larsen and von Ins (2010), Medoff (2006), and Collins (1998)

claim: In the 1960s, sociologists of science suggested that researchers would search for cues as to what literature to read in the midst of information overload.
source: Already in the 1960s, sociologists of science suggested that researchers, in the midst of this information overload, would search for cues as to what literature to read (Merton, 1968; Crane, 1965).
evidence: Supported by citations to Merton (1968) and Crane (1965)

claim: The author's location was identified as an important cue for what literature to read.
source: One important cue was the author's location.
evidence: Inferred from the preceding discussion of cues in the context of citations to Merton (1968) and Crane (1965)

claim: Academic affiliations cast a 'halo-effect' on scholarly work that amplifies the recognition of researchers based at prestigious institutions at the expense of authors from institutions and nations of lower status.
source: Academic affiliations would cast a "halo-effect" (Crane, 1967) on scholarly work that would amplify the recognition of researchers based at prestigious institutions at the expense of authors from institutions and nations of lower status.
evidence: Supported by citation to Crane (1967)

claim: The halo effect ties closely to the idea of the 'Matthew effect' in science.
source: This halo effect ties closely to the idea of the "Matthew effect" in science, i.e. "the accumulation of differential advantages for certain segments of the population [of researchers] that are not necessarily bound up with demonstrated differences in capacity" (Merton, 1988).
evidence: Supported by citation to Merton (1988) defining the Matthew effect

claim: Country- and institution-related halo effects may arise from stereotypic beliefs about the relative performance capacity of scientists working at more or less prestigious institutions.
source: From a social psychological perspective, country- and institution-related halo effects may arise from stereotypic beliefs about the relative performance capacity of scientists working at more or less prestigious institutions (Jost et al., 2009; Greenwald and Banaji, 1995; Ridgeway, 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to Jost et al. (2009), Greenwald and Banaji (1995), and Ridgeway (2001)

claim: According to status characteristics theory, a scientist's nationality or institutional affiliation can be considered 'status signals' that implicitly influence peer-evaluations when salient.
source: According to status characteristics theory, a scientist's nationality or institutional affiliation can be considered "status signals" that, when salient, implicitly influence peer-evaluations (Berger et al., 1977; Correll and Bernard, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Berger et al. (1977) and Correll and Bernard (2015)

claim: System justification theory asserts that members of a social hierarchy will feel motivated to see existing social arrangements as fair and justifiable to preserve a sense of predictability and certainty around their own position.
source: Moreover, system justification theory asserts that members of a social hierarchy, such as the scientific community, regardless of their position in this hierarchy, will feel motivated to see existing social arrangements as fair and justifiable to preserve a sense of predictability and certainty around their own position (Jost et al., 2004; Jost et al., 2002; Magee and Galinsky, 2008; Son Hing et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Jost et al. (2004), Jost et al. (2002), Magee and Galinsky (2008), and Son Hing et al. (2011)

claim: Both higher and lower status groups may internalize implicit behaviours and attitudes that favour higher-status groups.
source: As a result, both higher and lower status groups may internalize implicit behaviours and attitudes that favour higher-status groups (Jost, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jost (2013)

claim: Several observational studies have examined the influence of country- and institution-related halo effects in peer-reviewing.
source: Several observational studies have examined the influence of country- and institution-related halo effects in peer-reviewing (Crane, 1967; Link, 1998; Murray et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Crane (1967), Link (1998), and Murray et al. (2018)

claim: Most observational studies indicate slight advantages in favor of researchers from high status countries (such as the US or UK) and universities (such as Harvard University or Oxford University).
source: Most of them indicate slight advantages in favor of researchers from high status countries (such as the US or UK) and universities (such as Harvard University or Oxford University).
evidence: Inferred from the cited observational studies (Crane, 1967; Link, 1998; Murray et al., 2018)

claim: A key limitation of the observational literature on halo effects concerns the unobserved heterogeneity attributable to differences in quality.
source: However, a key limitation of this literature concerns the unobserved heterogeneity attributable to differences in quality.
evidence: Based on logical inference about the limitations of observational designs

claim: Non-experimental designs do not allow determination of the advantages enjoyed by scientists at high-status locations independent of their capabilities as scientists or the content and character of their work.
source: Non-experimental designs do not allow us to determine the advantages enjoyed by scientists at high-status locations independent of their capabilities as scientists, or the content and character of their work.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about the limitations of non-experimental research designs

claim: The study examined the impact of academic affiliations on scientific judgment, independent of manuscript quality.
source: Here we examine the impact of academic affiliations on scientific judgment, independent of manuscript quality.
evidence: This is the stated purpose of the experimental study described in the manuscript

claim: The study asked 4147 scientists from six disciplines to rate abstracts that vary on author country and institutional affiliation.
source: In a preregistered survey experiment, we asked 4147 scientists from six disciplines (astronomy, cardiology, materials science, political science, psychology and public health) to rate abstracts that vary on two factors: (i) author country (high status vs. lower status scientific nation); (ii) institutional affiliation (high status vs. lower status university; see Table 1).
evidence: This describes the experimental design and sample size of the study

claim: All other content of the discipline-specific abstracts was held constant.
source: All other content of the discipline-specific abstracts was held constant.
evidence: This describes the experimental control used in the study

claim: Blank (1991) found no evidence that a switch from single blind to double blind peer reviewing influenced the relative ratings of papers from high-ranked and lower-ranked universities.
source: One study (Blank, 1991) used a randomized field experiment to examine the effects of double blind vs. single blind peer reviewing on acceptance rates in the American Economic Review. The study found no evidence that a switch from single blind to double blind peer reviewing influenced the relative ratings of papers from high-ranked and lower-ranked universities.
evidence: Supported by citation to Blank (1991)

claim: Ross et al. (2006) found that when abstracts underwent single blind compared to double blind reviewing, the relative increase in acceptance rates was higher for US authored abstracts compared to non-US authored abstracts.
source: Another study (Ross et al., 2006) examined the effect of single blind vs. double blind peer reviewing on the assessment of 13,000 abstracts submitted to the American Heart Association's annual Scientific Sessions between 2000 and 2004. The study found that when abstracts underwent single blind compared to double blind reviewing the relative increase in acceptance rates was higher for US authored abstracts compared to non-US authored abstracts, and for abstracts from highly prestigious US institutions compared to abstracts from non-prestigious US institutions.
evidence: Supported by citation to Ross et al. (2006)

claim: Ross et al. (2006) found that when abstracts underwent single blind compared to double blind reviewing, the relative increase in acceptance rates was higher for abstracts from highly prestigious US institutions compared to abstracts from non-prestigious US institutions.
source: Another study (Ross et al., 2006) examined the effect of single blind vs. double blind peer reviewing on the assessment of 13,000 abstracts submitted to the American Heart Association's annual Scientific Sessions between 2000 and 2004. The study found that when abstracts underwent single blind compared to double blind reviewing the relative increase in acceptance rates was higher for US authored abstracts compared to non-US authored abstracts, and for abstracts from highly prestigious US institutions compared to abstracts from non-prestigious US institutions.
evidence: Supported by citation to Ross et al. (2006)

claim: Harris et al. (2015) found that professors at schools of public health in the US rated one abstract higher on likelihood of referral to a peer when the authors' affiliation was changed from a low-income to a high-income country.
source: A recent survey experiment also found that professors at schools of public health in the US (N: 899) rated one abstract higher on likelihood of referral to a peer, when the authors' affiliation was changed from a low-income to a high-income country (Harris et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Harris et al. (2015)

claim: Harris et al. (2015) found the results for three remaining abstracts were inconclusive.
source: However, each participant was asked to rate four abstracts and the results for the remaining three abstracts were inconclusive.
evidence: Supported by citation to Harris et al. (2015) in the preceding sentence

claim: Harris et al. (2015) found no evidence of country-related bias in the ratings of the strength of the evidence presented in the abstracts.
source: Likewise, the study found no evidence of country-related bias in the ratings of the strength of the evidence presented in the abstracts.
evidence: Supported by citation to Harris et al. (2015) in the preceding context

claim: Harris et al. (2017) found that changing the source of an abstract from a low-income to a high-income country slightly improved English clinicians' ratings of relevance and recommendation to a peer.
source: In another randomized, blinded cross-over study (N: 347), the same authors found that changing the source of an abstract from a low-income to a high-income country slightly improved English clinicians' ratings of relevance and recommendation to a peer (Harris et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Harris et al. (2017)

claim: Tomkins et al. (2017) found that single blind reviewers were more likely than double blind reviewers to accept papers from top-ranked universities compared to papers from lower-ranked universities.
source: Finally, a controlled field experiment recently examined the "within subject" effect of peer-review model (single blind vs. double blind) on the acceptance rates of full-length submissions for a prestigious computer-science conference (Tomkins et al., 2017). The study allocated 974 double blind and 983 single blind reviewers to 500 papers. Two single blind and two double blind reviewers assessed each paper. The study found that single blind reviewers were more likely than double blind reviewers to accept papers from top-ranked universities compared to papers from lower-ranked universities.
evidence: Supported by citation to Tomkins et al. (2017)

claim: The study contributes to pioneering work by targeting a broader range of disciplines in the social sciences, health sciences and natural sciences.
source: Our study contributes to this pioneering work by targeting a broader range of disciplines in the social sciences, health sciences and natural sciences.
evidence: This describes the contribution of the current study relative to prior work

claim: The study allows examination of possible between-discipline variation in the prevalence of country- or institution-related rater bias.
source: This allows us to examine possible between-discipline variation in the prevalence of country- or institution-related rater bias.
evidence: This describes the analytical capability enabled by the multi-discipline design

claim: The six discipline-specific experiments show weak and inconsistent evidence of country- or institution-related status bias in abstract ratings.
source: Our six discipline-specific experiments show weak and inconsistent evidence of country- or institution-related status bias in abstract ratings, and mixed regression models indicate that any plausible effect must be small in size.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study based on experimental data

claim: Mixed regression models indicate that any plausible effect of country- or institution-related status bias must be small in size.
source: Our six discipline-specific experiments show weak and inconsistent evidence of country- or institution-related status bias in abstract ratings, and mixed regression models indicate that any plausible effect must be small in size.
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical analysis of the experimental data

claim: The analysis took place in two steps: first using ANOVAs and logit models for discipline-specific analyses, and second using mixed regression models with disciplines as random effect parameter.
source: In accordance with our preregistered plan (see https://osf.io/4gjwa), the analysis took place in two steps. First, we used ANOVAs and logit models to conduct discipline-specific analyses of how country- and institution-related status signals influence scholarly judgments made by peer-evaluators. Second, we employed mixed regression models with disciplines as random effect parameter to estimate the direct effect and moderation effects of the presumed association between status signals and evaluative outcomes at an aggregate, cross-disciplinary level.
evidence: This describes the analytical approach used in the study

claim: Abstract score consists of four items recorded on a five-point scale that ask peer-evaluators to assess the originality of the presented research, the credibility of the results, the significance for future research, and the clarity and comprehensiveness of the abstract.
source: Abstract score is our main outcome variable. It consists of four items recorded on a five-point scale (1="very poor", 5 = "excellent") that ask the peer-evaluators to assess (i) the originality of the presented research, (ii) the credibility of the results, (iii) the significance for future research, and (iv) the clarity and comprehensiveness of the abstract.
evidence: This describes the measurement of the main outcome variable

claim: A composite measure was computed that specifies each participant's total-item score for the four abstract rating items (Cronbach's α = 0.778).
source: We computed a composite measure that specifies each participant's total-item score for these four items (Cronbach's α = 0.778).
evidence: This describes the construction and reliability of the composite outcome measure

claim: Open full-text is a dichotomous outcome measure that asks whether the peer-evaluator would choose to open the full text and continue reading if they came across the abstract online.
source: Open full-text is a dichotomous outcome measure that asks whether the peer-evaluator would choose to open the full text and continue reading, if s/he came across the abstract online.
evidence: This describes one of the outcome measures used in the study

claim: Include in conference is a dichotomous outcome measure that asks whether the peer-evaluator would choose to include the abstract for an oral presentation if they were reviewing it as a committee member of a selective international scientific conference.
source: Include in conference is a dichotomous outcome measure that asks whether the peer-evaluator would choose to include the abstract for an oral presentation, if s/he was reviewing it as a committee member of a selective international scientific conference (the full questionnaire is included in the Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This describes one of the outcome measures used in the study

claim: G*Power was used to calculate the required sample size per discipline (N = 429) for detecting a Cohen's f = 0.15 or larger with α = 0.05 and a power of 0.80.
source: As specified in the registered plan, we used G*Power to calculate the required sample size per discipline (N = 429) for detecting a Cohen's f = 0.15 (corresponding to a Cohen's d = 0.30) or larger with α = 0.05 and a power of 0.80 in the cross-group comparisons with abstract score as outcome.
evidence: This describes the power analysis conducted for the study

source: As displayed in Figure 2, peer-evaluators in Public Health were between 7.5% and 56.5% less likely to show interest in opening the full-text, when the author affiliation was changed from a lower-status university in the US to a lower-status university elsewhere (Odds ratio:. 634, CI: 0.435–0.925).

claim: In five of the 12 between-subject comparisons for Open full-text, the direction of the observed effects was inconsistent with the a-priori expectation that abstracts from higher-status US universities would be favoured over abstracts from lower-status US universities, and that abstracts from lower-status US universities would be favoured over abstracts from lower-status universities elsewhere.
source: Moreover, in five of the 12 between-subject comparisons, the direction of the observed effects was inconsistent with the a-priori expectation that abstracts from higher-status US universities would be favoured over abstracts from lower-status US universities, and that abstracts from lower-status US universities would be favoured over abstracts from lower-status universities elsewhere.
evidence: This is a summary of the direction of effects from the statistical analyses

source: As displayed in Figure 3, peer-evaluators in political science were between 7.0% and 59.4% less likely to consider an abstract relevant for a selective, international conference program, when the abstract's author was affiliated with a higher-status US university compared to a lower-status US university (Odds ratio:. 613, CI:. 406-.930).

source: Figure 4 plots the fixed coefficients (panel a) and adjusted means (panel b) from the mixed linear regression with Abstract rating as outcome. In accordance with the pre-registered analysis plan, we report the mixed regression models with 99% confidence intervals. The fixed coefficients for the two between-group comparisons tested in this model are close to zero, and the 99% confidence intervals suggest that any plausible difference would fall within the bounds of −0.26 to 0.28 points on the 16-point abstract-rating scale.
evidence: This is a result from the mixed linear regression analysis shown in Figure 4

claim: Robustness checks based on mixed linear and logit models restricting samples to participants that responded correctly to a manipulation-check item yielded qualitatively similar results with small residual effects and confidence intervals spanning 0 in the linear regressions and one in the logistic regressions.
source: Robustness checks based on mixed linear and logit models were carried out to examine the effects of the experimental manipulations on the three outcome measures, while restricting the samples to (i) participants that responded correctly to a manipulation-check item, and (ii) participants that saw their own research as being 'extremely close', 'very close' or 'somewhat close' to the subject addressed in the abstract. All of these models yielded qualitatively similar results, with small residual effects and confidence intervals spanning 0 in the linear regressions and one in the logistic regressions (see Supplementary file 2, Tables S28–S33).
evidence: This is a result from the robustness check analyses

claim: Robustness checks based on mixed linear and logit models restricting samples to participants that saw their own research as being 'extremely close', 'very close' or 'somewhat close' to the subject addressed in the abstract yielded qualitatively similar results with small residual effects and confidence intervals spanning 0 in the linear regressions and one in the logistic regressions.
source: Robustness checks based on mixed linear and logit models were carried out to examine the effects of the experimental manipulations on the three outcome measures, while restricting the samples to (i) participants that responded correctly to a manipulation-check item, and (ii) participants that saw their own research as being 'extremely close', 'very close' or 'somewhat close' to the subject addressed in the abstract. All of these models yielded qualitatively similar results, with small residual effects and confidence intervals spanning 0 in the linear regressions and one in the logistic regressions (see Supplementary file 2, Tables S28–S33).

claim: All two-way interactions examining whether the influence of country- and institution-related status signals was moderated by characteristics of the peer evaluators had 99% CI intervals spanning 0 in the linear regressions and one in the logistic regressions, indicating no discernible two-way interactions.
source: Moreover, a pre-registered interaction analysis was conducted to examine whether the influence of country- and institution-related status signals was moderated by any of the following characteristics of the peer evaluators: (i) their descriptive beliefs in the objectivity and fairness of peer-evaluation; (ii) their structural location in the science system (in terms of institutional affiliation and scientific rank); (iii) their research accomplishments; (iv) their self-perceived scientific status. All of these two-way interactions had 99% CI intervals spanning 0 in the linear regressions and one in the logistic regressions, indicating no discernible two-way interactions (see Supplementary file 2, Tables S34–S39).
evidence: This is a result from the interaction analyses

claim: The study shows weak and inconsistent evidence of country- or institution-related status bias in abstract ratings, contrary to the idea of halo effects.
